dossier.mechanism: Every Millrace level is a closed delivery problem. You get a fixed board, the whole arrival queue of 2s and 4s visible before move one, a single marked inlet that must stay clear, and one vault cell that must hold an exact value within a move budget. Every level was found by search and solved exhaustively, so its shortest solution is a proven number. A level was thrown away if any of 280 no-lookahead strategies could win it, or if random play won more than 2% of the time. The six chapters are pinned to that proven depth: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, then 10 or more moves.
dossier.audienceScene: A puzzle player on an iPhone, on a commute or a flight or in bed. They arrive from Google or an AI answer for 'games like Threes', 'logic puzzle game no ads', 'puzzle game with a solution', or an alternatives query (Threes, KAMI 2, Flow Free, Two Dots, Suika Game). Often they are tired of saga games that sell lives and boosters. Within seconds they want to know what a level asks, that it is free with no ads and no account, and that the levels have real depth. Desktop visitors, often coming from the journal essay on how the levels are made, need the QR to get it onto an iPhone or iPad.
dossier.culturalHome: Deterministic single-player logic puzzles and the people who chase optimal solutions. That includes boxed puzzle games with graded challenge cards, Sokoban level sets, KAMI's move-count 'Perfect', and Threes and the 2048 slide-and-merge lineage, as well as speedcubing's fewest-moves culture and golf's par. Its own vocabulary is the developer's, from the journal: the generator, the exhaustive breadth-first solver, 'the gate', the 'vault', sixteen checks, 280 thoughtless players, 'a puzzle needs a way to go wrong'. The name and icon point at water: a millrace is a mill's channel, and the icon draws one, a walnut channel with a red-orange bar, a green bar and an amber block between them.
dossier.mustProve: That a level is a closed problem with a proven answer. The first viewport must show the arrival queue in full, the exact target and the budget. The real example is Level 58 in screenshot 1: build exactly 64 on the marked cell, 8 moves left, queue 2 4 2 4 4 4. It must also say that every level's shortest solution is proven before it ships. Alongside that: free in full (price.value 'Free — optional theme packs & undo tokens'), no ads, no account, the working App Store badge, and the QR on desktop.
dossier.categoryDefault: The mobile-puzzle landing page: a candy gradient or a dark glossy backdrop, bouncy rounded type, floating 3D tiles and confetti, a centred phone mockup, a laurel-and-stars 'Addictive!' strip, a stat row and a feature-card grid. 2048-likes add a beige-and-orange tile grid in a rounded sans. The incumbent already ships a version of this: cream page, serif H1 on the left, amber gameplay phone on the right, a badge row.
dossier.predictableOpposite: Zen-puzzle minimalism: a white or pastel void, a thin geometric sans, one floating isometric tile and 'calm' copy. Or its engineering twin, the 'proof' page: a black terminal, monospaced solver logs and green PASSED badges.
dossier.literalReading: The millrace itself: a timber channel carrying water to a mill wheel, with sluice gates, the wheel and flowing water. The icon already depicts it (walnut channel, two coloured cross-bars, an amber block). Only candidate 7 uses it.

Mechanic (quick_answer, body, features[1]): fixed board, visible queue, single marked inlet, one exact value on one marked cell, move budget. Two ways to lose: block the inlet, or overshoot (a 128 when it asked for 64). Freeplay is the endless board with a daily board and streaks.

Proof facts (how_it_works, body, journal how-millrace-levels-are-made): exhaustive BFS proves the shortest solution. All 280 no-lookahead strategies must fail. Random-play odds are computed exactly with a 2% ceiling: 1.31% on Level 1, about 1 in 1,000 at the median, about 1 in a million on the deepest. One to eight candidates in 1,000 survive. Sixteen checks live in the test suite. The deepest level needs all 16 of its 16 moves.

Chapter table (journal), as levels / shortest / budget: Warm-up 4 / exactly 5 / 7; Tactics 12 / 6 / 8; Pressure 12 / 7 / 8–9; Precision 12 / 8 / 9–10; Deep Water 12 / 9 / 9–11; Mastery 12 / 10–16 / 12–16. Par subtotals follow: 20, 72, 84, 96, 108.

A green bar sits beside the cell ghosting the 64 (the vault) and a red-orange bar at the opposite edge (the inlet). The colour roles are inferred from the screenshot and match the icon.

candidates.name: The challenge-card deck
candidates.why: Boxed logic puzzles such as Rush Hour (1996) taught a generation the format: a numbered challenge card, colour tiers from Beginner to Expert, the solution on the back. It carries the mechanism directly. Each level becomes a card whose front is the closed problem (board, inlet, vault, queue, target, budget) and whose back is the proof (proven shortest solution, exact random-play odds, 280 of 280 strategies failed). The six tiers are the six depth chapters, and the deck's edge shows their real sizes (4 + 12×5).

candidates.name: The gamebook ('turn to 58')
candidates.why: Choose Your Own Adventure (1979–) and Fighting Fantasy (1982–) made numbered, branching sections a shared memory. Because nothing in a level is random, a whole Millrace line can be printed as linked sections. Every wrong choice ends ('the inlet is blocked — the end'), and one line reaches the vault in the proven minimum. The Adventure Sheet becomes the target, queue and budget boxes, and the whole thing plays with plain anchor links.

candidates.name: The Hakone puzzle box (himitsu-bako)
candidates.why: Japanese secret boxes are sold by step count (4, 7, 10, 21 moves to open) and wrapped in yosegi marquetry, so collectors buy depth, just as Millrace pins chapters to 5–10+ moves. Each chapter becomes a box of known step count whose panels slide in an order you cannot guess, and the icon's sliding block reads as one panel. Sibling watch: Shogiful also works in Japanese timber.

candidates.name: The sounding chart
candidates.why: Admiralty and NOAA charts print measured depths as soundings and contour each depth, and most people recognise the scatter of numbers on pale blue. It carries 'the difficulty curve is search depth'. The scroll descends through six depth contours (5 to 10+), each level is plotted as a sounding, and 'Deep Water' is already a chapter name. The board becomes a harbour inset with the inlet as its mouth.

candidates.name: Fewest Moves and God's Number
candidates.why: Speedcubing's Fewest Moves event hands out a printed scramble and scores your written solution by move count. In 2010 an exhaustive computer search proved that every cube position solves in 20 moves or fewer. It carries the mechanism: the scramble is the fixed start, and your line is scored against a computer-proven optimum, which is exactly what the result card's 'Best possible is X moves' means.

candidates.name: The scorecard and yardage book
candidates.why: Everyone knows par, and the app's own body copy says 'the par you are chasing is a computed fact'. It carries the mechanism as a 64-hole scorecard. The PAR row is the proven shortest solution (5, 5, 5, 5, then sixes, through 10–16) and the MAX row is the budget. Chapters become loops with subtotals (Tactics: 12 × 6 = par 72), and the yardage book's measured drawings carry 'measured, not claimed'. Tee red and the green match the app's inlet and vault markers.

candidates.name: The millrace itself
candidates.why: This is the name's own object, and the icon already draws it: a walnut-lined race, a red-orange cross-bar, a green cross-bar and an amber block riding between. It carries the FAQ's own explanation ('a steady flow arriving at one point… keep the channel clear while you build the delivery'). The sluice is the journal's 'gate', which roughly one to eight candidates in a thousand pass, and the race's staff gauge reads depth. This is the list's single literal candidate.

styles.label: The Amber Race
styles.lineage: The mill race as built, seen from directly above, which is exactly what the app icon draws: the plank-lined headrace from weir to wheel, its sluice gate set in stop-log grooves, the staff gauge bolted to the race wall, the miller's painted toll board. Water colour comes from the app's own amber-liquid level screens (screenshots 1, 3, 5) and from peat-stained races that run tea-amber. The FAQ supplies the mapping: 'a steady flow arriving at one point… keep the channel clear while you build the delivery.' This is the list's one literal reading, committed fully.
styles.thesis: The page is one millrace followed downstream. You enter at the red-orange inlet gate, where the queue of arriving tiles waits and the download sits, and the page flows reach by reach to the green vault gate where the delivery is made: the icon scaled into a site. It refuses the category's glossy phone-in-a-gradient hero and the incumbent's copy-left/phone-right split.

styles.navigation: The headrace beam: wordmark and icon (linking to top) and five anchor links set into the walnut in #F7E4BF type. On mobile a 'Menu' peg opens a <details> drop, a walnut board hanging under the beam with the same links at 20px, and needs no JS. The beam scrolls away with the page; the sticky inlet bar is the only pinned element. Focus is a 3px #1F1209 ring with a 2px #F7E4BF gap on water, inverted on walnut.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'The gate.' In the how_it_works reach, one inline SVG holds 1,000 tiny amber squares, one per candidate level, floating upstream of four stop-log grooves. Each step is a stop-log. As a step scrolls into view, IntersectionObserver adds .seated and its log drops 24px into the groove in 220ms. When the fourth is seated, the field sinks to 6% opacity except a handful of squares that pass under the gate and stay lit, captioned 'Roughly one to eight candidates in a thousand survive, depending on the chapter.' Which squares pass is illustrative and labelled so. No-JS: the logs render seated, the field already sunk, the survivors lit, and every step's text present. Reduced motion: final state at once, no drops.
styles.motionGrammar: Everything moves downstream or not at all. In the hero reach only, the caustic layer drifts down 1,400px in 40s (linear, looping) and the queue tiles bob 2px on a 6s ease-in-out loop. Stop-logs drop once, vertically, and the sticky inlet bar rises from the bottom edge in 220ms. Beams, gauge and text never animate, and nothing fades in on scroll. prefers-reduced-motion: still water, static tiles, logs already seated.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and the five alternatives pages (Threes, KAMI 2, Flow Free, Two Dots, Suika Game) are a quieter side race: the same walnut walls and headrace beam nav. The page title sits on a walnut beam (Rokkitt 800, 44px / 30px). The reading column is the shallows (#F0C77A) in Alegreya Sans 400 19px/1.65 at 66ch, ink 11.5:1, with no caustics and no tiles. Alternatives pages open with two short beams naming each game and what it asks ('Millrace: deliver one exact value' / 'Threes: survive an endless board'). The table is set on oak with walnut heads, the FAQ is <details> rows split by plank seams, and the page closes on a small inlet beam with the badge. Privacy opens with the staff gauge reading the transparency row, linked to /transparency/. Support is the millwright's plate: email, response time and restore-purchase steps.
styles.assetsNeeded: None. Walls, water, beams, logs, gauge and tiles are CSS and inline SVG. It uses assets/icons/millrace.png, the nine screenshots and assets/qr/millrace.svg. The board replica copies only what screenshot 1 shows (Level 58 mid-game) and is captioned as such.
styles.risk: This is the literal reading. It can tip into theme-park water and turn the page into a picture of the icon, so every reach must work as set text on water, with beams carrying real headings and actions. A long amber drench tires the eye on dense sections, which is why tables and FAQ answers move to oak and shallows. The world sits close to the app's own amber screens; that helps recognition but risks reading as one giant screenshot. The narrow single channel leaves wide desktop margins quiet by design. A linen bank must never creep in, or the page falls into the cream cluster.
styles.memoryTest: A website that was a wooden water channel full of amber water. Numbered tiles were queued against a red-orange gate where the download button was, and a green gate at the bottom 'delivered' it to my phone. A thousand little squares went into the sluice and about eight came out.

styles.label: Turn the Card
styles.lineage: Boxed single-player logic games and their challenge decks, such as Binary Arts/ThinkFun's Rush Hour (1996) and its stablemates. One board and a deck of numbered challenge cards graded in colour tiers from Beginner to Expert, setup on the front and solution on the back, in a vacuum-formed tray inside the box with a folded rule sheet. Lineage only: no ThinkFun names, trade dress or card art.
styles.thesis: Every Millrace level is a challenge card whose front is the closed problem and whose back is its proof. The page lays one card on the box tray, lets you turn it over, and unfolds the rule sheet beneath. It refuses the phone-mockup hero: the product's real claim, a proven shortest solution, is printed on the back of a card.
styles.scene: A kitchen table by a window in daylight, the game box open on its cobalt plastic tray and the first card already dealt on white card stock. Light scheme (color-scheme: light): the tray is a saturated mid-dark ground, but every reading surface is white card.

styles.signatureInteraction: 'Turn it over.' The hero card is a <button aria-pressed> holding two faces. Click, tap or Enter turns it on the Y axis (CSS 3D, rotateY 180°, 520ms, perspective 1200px) to reveal the back. The back reads: 'Shortest solution: 5 moves, proven by breadth-first search over every position. Budget: 7. Random play wins this card 1.31% of the time, computed exactly. All 280 thoughtless strategies fail it.' It carries the green 'proven' seal, and a second press turns it back. The fanned tier cards turn the same way to show each chapter's depth and budget. No-JS: without html.js, front and back render as two cards side by side (stacked on mobile) labelled 'Front' and 'Back' on the tray, so every word is visible. Reduced motion: the faces swap with no rotation.
styles.motionGrammar: Cards move like cards. A turn is on the Y axis (520ms, cubic-bezier(.3,.7,.2,1)). On first view the six tier cards deal from the deck's position along a short arc, 60ms apart and 260ms each (html.js only; the static fan is the default), and the sticky rim strip rises in 200ms. Nothing loops, floats or parallaxes. prefers-reduced-motion: no deal, and the turn becomes an instant face swap.

styles.assetsNeeded: Data, not art: the start position (board, inlet edge cell, vault cell, arrival queue) of Level 1 and of one level per chapter for the tier fan, exported from the app's level library. Until then, Card 1's diagram takes its tiles from the Level 1 thumbnail in screenshot 2, the three queue boxes show the count only, and the inlet and vault placement carries a printed 'illustrative layout' note. Every other card fact is already sourced: target 16, 3 arriving, shortest 5, budget 7, random 1.31%. Otherwise it uses the existing icon, screenshots and QR.
styles.risk: Familiar: a challenge-card deck is the first physical analogue anyone reaches for with a level-based puzzle. That is why it tops the list and also why it is the least surprising, and ThinkFun's trade dress must be kept at arm's length. Six tier colours on a cobalt tray can read juvenile, louder than the studio's calm voice. The card diagram is only as honest as the level data behind it, and the turn is the page's single proof device, so it must stay fast and keyboard-operable. The triptych hero must not collapse into a copy/product split at mid widths.

styles.lineage: Golf's paper: the club scorecard and the tour yardage book. The scorecard has HOLE, YARDS, PAR and STROKE INDEX rows, OUT and IN subtotal columns, the marker's and player's signature boxes, and local rules printed on the back. The yardage book is a pocket book with a measured plan of every hole and distances pencilled to the yard. It is grounded in the app's own copy, 'the par you are chasing is a computed fact rather than an estimate'. Tee red and the green are the app's inlet and vault colours.
styles.thesis: The page is the scorecard for a 64-hole course whose par was computed, not assigned. The hero prints the PAR row across all 64 holes (five, five, five, five, then twelve sixes, through to 10–16), and the rest of the page is the back of the card and the yardage book. It refuses the gradient-and-phone puzzle page for a document a player fills in with a pencil.

type.rationale: About 60 KB across four files. A condensed gothic plus News Gothic is how scorecards are actually printed, and the pencil marks the one thing on a card that is not printed. No sibling uses any of the three.

styles.navigation: The card's header strip: wordmark and five uppercase anchor links in Antonio 700, green on white, with a 2px green underline on hover and focus. It is not sticky; the box-row bar is the only pinned element. On mobile, 'Menu' opens a <details> panel ruled like a card row, with the links at 20px. Focus is a 3px #1C5B3A outline with a 2px white offset everywhere, and focusable table cells also take the fairway fill.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'Hole by hole.' Every hole number on THE CARD is a focusable button. Hovering, focusing or tapping one fills its column fairway-green, drops a flag-yellow marker above it, and writes a readout under the card such as 'Hole 23 · Pressure · par 7, proven · max 8–9'. The readout uses chapter values now, and per-hole target, arrivals, exact budget and random-play odds once the level table is supplied. Arrow keys move along the row. Chapter brackets jump to the yardage pages, and holes 1, 44 and 58 have full pages. No-JS: the card is a complete, readable <table> with th scope, the readout line shows the key statically, and the links still jump. Reduced motion: the column fills with no transition.
styles.motionGrammar: Paper does not move. The only motion: the hole-column fill (120ms), the flag marker settling 6px (160ms) and the sticky box row sliding up (200ms). The readout swaps text with no animation. There are no scroll reveals and no counters. prefers-reduced-motion: fills and the sticky row appear instantly.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and the five alternatives pages are the back of the card: the same header strip, then the title in Antonio 700 uppercase green (48px / 32px) under a crease. The reading column is the card itself in News Cycle 400 18px/1.65 at 66ch, black ink 17.9:1, with section heads in Antonio 700 28px green and tables ruled like the scorecard. Alternatives pages open with a two-player card: 'MILLRACE | THREES' columns with the rows What a game asks · Measure of success · Ads · Price · Privacy label, and a fairway fill on Millrace's column. After it come the existing comparison, the verdict as 'Play Millrace if / Play Threes if' columns, FAQ <details> and a DOWNLOAD box. Privacy opens with a 'Local rule' box that reads the transparency row and links to /transparency/. Support is 'Ask the starter': email, response time and restore-purchase steps.
styles.assetsNeeded: Data, not art: the 64-row level table (target, arrivals, proven shortest, budget, random-play odds) and the start positions of Levels 1 and 44, exported from the app's level library. Until then the card prints only what is already sourced: par by chapter (exactly 5 to 9; 10–16 for Mastery), max by chapter range, and the subtotals. The yardage pages draw only the tiles visible in screenshots 1, 2 and 4, with inlet and vault placement marked 'illustrative layout' where not visible. Otherwise it uses the existing icon, nine screenshots and QR.
styles.risk: Golf is a borrowed world with country-club connotations a puzzle audience may not share, and the metaphor has seams. The move budget is not golf's maximum-score rule, so the card must define Par and Max right under the grid. A 64-hole row is dense at 1440 (~16px cells), and the page depends on folding cleanly into chapter strips on mobile. An uppercase condensed H1 can shout against the studio's calm voice. If the rules, folds and pencil are weak, white card and green ink collapse into a generic form.
styles.memoryTest: A golf scorecard for a 64-hole course. The par row went five, five, five, five, then sixes and sevens, and it said par was proven by a computer. Tactics plays to par 72, and the download button was in the signature box.

canon: Canon (the category played straight; not recommended): a molten-amber gradient page with glossy 3D tiles floating around a centred iPhone playing Level 58. Above it, 'Sixty-four levels. One inlet. Nothing is random.' with the App Store badge and QR. Below, a four-stat row (64 levels · 6 chapters · 17 themes · 0 ads), a feature-card grid, the comparison table, then the FAQ.
notes: Degraded roll: the roll service was unreachable, so there were no catalog challengers and no quality-bar boards. Key 214d9de3, assigned index 7, re-roll 1 = 6 (distinct on the first try). The candidate order was fixed before the roll. Mapping: A = candidate 7 (THE ROLL; the list's single literal reading, committed in full), B = candidate 1 (IMPECCABLE’S PICK, since neither N nor R1 is 1), C = candidate 6 (SECOND ROLL). Fonts were verified on Fontsource 5.3.0 via npm pack, latin woff2 per weight: Rokkitt 100–900 (~13 KB each), Alegreya Sans 100/300/400/500/700/800/900 (~24 KB), Gabarito 400–900 (~20 KB), Figtree 300–900 (~11 KB), Antonio 100–700 (~11 KB), News Cycle 400/700 (~13 KB), Kalam 300/400/700 (~22 KB). Per-page budgets are about 110 KB (A), 63 KB (B) and 60 KB (C). None of these faces appears in the sibling boards written so far (I deliberately avoided Public Sans, Albert Sans and the Big Shoulders family, which siblings already use). Facts the build must respect: (1) Inlet and vault colours are inferred from screenshot 1 (green bar beside the cell ghosting the 64 = vault; red-orange bar = inlet) and match the icon; confirm with the developer before any diagram ships. (2) Per-level start positions, queues and exact budgets are not in the repo, so B's card diagrams and C's per-hole rows need a level-table export; until then they show only sourced facts and say 'illustrative layout'. (3) Copy says 34 languages / 40 locales, but app_enrichment.yml lists 33 language codes; reconcile. (4) The founder signal '19 live apps' is a literal that matches today's 19 status: live apps; keep it in sync or compute. (5) hero.pre_headline and the founder/example_insights overlines must never render as eyebrows; each style folds them into a descriptor or drops them. (6) No testimonials and no ratings exist for Millrace, so no stars or quotes appear anywhere. (7) redirect_from /apps/zen-2048/ and /apps/calm-2048/ must survive the rebuild. Sibling watch: A's amber drench shares warmth with Allpaid's yellow poster and EarnLock's amber LED digits, but it is a water channel, not a sign or a display. B's cobalt tray and C's white-and-green scorecard collide with no board written so far. Candidate 3 (Hakone box) was flagged against Shogiful's Japanese-timber world and was not dealt.
